newsitem.title: UK: EBRD sees foreign investors trickling into Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: EBRD sees foreign investors trickling into Bosnia.

text.p: Foreign investment is beginning to trickle into Bosnia after its devastating 3-1/2 year war, lured chiefly by pledges of billions of dollars of international aid, but business so far has been on a small scale.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) said it was aware of around 100 recent joint ventures involving a handful of neighbouring countries along with Italy, Germany, Austria and Greece.

"It's very difficult to fight against the image of the country," Zsuzanna Hargitai, the EBRD's deputy resident representative in Sarajevo, told Reuters in an interview in London. It's the war image, it's lack of information, it's physical access. On the other hand, companies are lured to Bosnia-Herzegovina by the donor programme and the possibility of the new contracts they might get under it. They might get a feel for the country and invest."
The Bosnian war ended in 1995 with the U.S.-brokered Dayton Accords. The international community pledged $5.1 billion over three to four years to help rebuild the shattered economy.

But a donors' conference aimed at raising $1.4 billion has been postponed twice because Bosnia's central government, comprised of representatives of former warring Serb, Croat and Moslem factions, has failed to implement economic reform.
Hargitai said foreign investment so far has been mainly in small and medium-sized companies in sectors such as food and wood processing, clothing and sportswear.

"For the time being it's contractors and traders," she said. "There is surprisingly good interest from the neighbouring region -- Croatia, Slovenia and Hungary. People from the region are less frightened."
Among larger potential foreign investors, German industrial giants Siemens AG and Volkswagen AG are involved in exploratory talks about operating in Bosnia, she added, without giving details.
Bertram Reddig of the German Savings Banks Association said he had been surprised by the level of interest among German small and medium-sized enterprises.
"Among our clients, there is, amazingly, relatively large interest in going to Bosnia and doing business there, even investing in repair shops for buses and things like that," he said.
But there was concern about the lack of transparency in the procedure for tendering for reconstruction projects, he said.
Franz Krejs of Vienna-based Horizonte Venture Management said his company had begun looking for business in Sarajevo the day after the Dayton Accords were signed.

It aims to invest both in local firms and in joint ventures involving foreign companies. "We already have about 20 projects on our desk from Austria, the Netherlands and Germany," he told Reuters. "Interest is relatively strong."
Fears of a resumption of war in what is still a politically unstable country was a deterrent to investors.
"But what primarily interests people is that Bosnia is different from other east European countries because an enormous volume of aid money is flowing in," Krejs said.
His fund aims to ensure that at least some of the aid filters down to local enterprises.
Krejs says it will take a minimum of five years before some degree of economic normality returns to Bosnia, provided fighting does not resume.
"There is considerable enterpreneurial potential down there -- people really want to do something," he said.

Hargitai said uncertainty about the legal and regulatory framework -- some of it dating back to the communist era -- is a problem, but she advises investors to "take a take a deep plunge. "It is not clear, but it's survivable," she said.
